objectives: State the CAP theorem and explain why "CA" is essentially a myth in distributed systems.
What does "consistency" mean in CAP, and how does it differ from "consistency" in ACID?
Why is Cassandra classified as AP, and how does it converge after a partition heals?
Why is MongoDB classified as CP, and what happens during a primary failover?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** The CAP theorem (Brewer, 2000; Gilbert-Lynch proof, 2002) states that a distributed system can simultaneously guarantee at most **two** of three properties — **Consistency** (linearizability), **Availability** (every request gets a response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps operating despite network splits) — and because partitions are unavoidable in real networks, the practical choice is between **CP** (sacrifice availability) and **AP** (sacrifice strong consistency).

CAP is the most quoted — and most misunderstood — theorem in distributed systems. Eric Brewer formulated it in 2000 as a conjecture based on observations at Inktomi; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch of MIT proved it formally in 2002. The theorem says: in a distributed system that replicates state across nodes connected by an asynchronous network, you cannot simultaneously provide all three of *Consistency* (every read sees the latest write or returns an error — i.e., the system behaves like a single copy), *Availability* (every non-failing node returns a non-error response in finite time), and *Partition tolerance* (the system keeps operating when the network drops or delays messages between nodes). Because real networks *do* drop and delay messages — switch failures, router misconfigurations, split-brain DNS, fiber cuts — partition tolerance is not optional. So the real choice is: when a partition happens, do you refuse some requests to preserve consistency (CP), or do you serve them and risk returning stale data (AP)?

Why does CAP matter? Because every distributed database makes this choice, often silently, and the choice determines what your application can guarantee to users. If you build a payment system on an AP store, you can return a stale balance and overdraw an account. If you build a social-feed "likes" counter on a CP store, every partition halts writes during the failure window — your users see "service unavailable" because of a transient network blip. Knowing the trade-off *before* you pick a database is the difference between a system that fits its SLO and one that doesn't.

Real-world examples are everywhere. **Cassandra** is the canonical AP system: it was inspired by Amazon's 2007 Dynamo paper and is designed for "always writable" workloads. During a partition, every replica accepts writes locally with a timestamp-based last-writer-wins resolution; reads may return stale data until repair converges. This made Cassandra a natural fit for Instagram's feed metadata and Netflix's viewing-history store, where availability and write throughput matter more than millisecond-strong consistency. **MongoDB**, by contrast, is CP-ish: a replica set has a single elected primary, and if the primary cannot reach a majority of the secondary nodes, it steps down and refuses writes until a new primary is elected. This guarantees that only one primary exists at a time (preventing split-brain writes), at the cost of write unavailability during elections — typically 10–30 seconds.

**Amazon's Dynamo paper** is the original articulation of the AP design philosophy. DynamoDB (the commercial product) is also AP: it sacrifices strong consistency by default, offering "eventual consistency" reads, though it does provide an optional "strongly consistent read" against a single replica when the read is sent to the leader of the key's preference list. The Amazon paper explicitly framed the trade-off: for the shopping cart, availability matters more than consistency — a temporarily stale cart is preferable to a cart that won't accept updates.

A second real-world example is **Kubernetes' use of etcd** as its backing store — a textbook CP system. etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm to ensure that only one leader accepts writes at a time, and a write must be acknowledged by a quorum of etcd members before it is committed. When an etcd member is partitioned away from the quorum, it cannot accept writes — preserving strong consistency of cluster state (which nodes exist, which pods are scheduled, which secrets are deployed). This is the right choice for Kubernetes because split-brain on cluster state would be catastrophic: two schedulers assigning the same pod to different nodes, or two controllers believing they own the same service. The cost is that during an etcd leader election (typically 1–2 seconds) the Kubernetes control plane is briefly read-only — no new deployments, no scaling operations. K8s operators accept this trade-off because the API server can still serve reads from cache and workloads keep running on existing schedulers.

A complementary AP example is **WhatsApp's message delivery path**, which uses a Dynamo-style AP store for user presence and message routing metadata. During a network partition, every regional cluster keeps accepting "user online" updates and routing decisions locally, so users can keep sending messages even when inter-region links are degraded. The system reconciles presence state after the partition heals using last-writer-wins on timestamps. This makes WhatsApp resilient to regional outages — a partition between datacenters does not prevent users from messaging — at the cost of brief presence-state inconsistency. For a chat application where a missed "user is online" indicator is trivial, the AP trade-off is clearly correct; for a banking ledger it would be catastrophic. The right CAP class depends entirely on the cost of inconsistency for that specific workload.

A common pitfall is treating CAP as a binary "you must pick CP or AP forever." In reality, most modern systems are *tunable*. Cassandra offers consistency levels from `ONE` (fastest, weakest) to `QUORUM` (read+write quorum gives strong consistency) to `ALL` (slowest, strongest). Mongo offers `writeConcern: {w: 1}` vs `{w: "majority"}`. Spanner uses Paxos to provide CP *and* high availability through its carefully engineered TrueTime clocks. PACELC (Topic 11) is the modern refinement that says: even *without* a partition, you choose between latency and consistency. So CAP is the starting point — not the final word.

Another pitfall is the **"CA" myth** — the idea that you can build a CA system by simply ignoring partitions. In a single-node database (Postgres on one machine) there is no partition to worry about, so the question is moot. But the moment you replicate across nodes, you have a partition-tolerance requirement, and you are now CP or AP. The "CA" label is meaningful only for non-distributed systems, which is why you should treat it as a red flag when a vendor claims it.

CAP connects to nearly every other concept in this phase. It is the formalization of the **availability vs consistency** trade-off that underlies every choice about **replication** (sync vs async), **durability** (quorum vs one), **latency** (sync replication increases latency), **throughput** (quorum writes reduce throughput), and **fault tolerance** (the theorem is fundamentally about what survives a fault). It is also the gateway to **PACELC**, which extends CAP to cover the no-partition case.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P[Network Partition Occurs]
    P --> Q{Choose one to sacrifice}

    Q -->|Sacrifice Availability| CP[CP System]
    Q -->|Sacrifice Consistency| AP[AP System]

    CP --> CP1[Block writes until partition heals]
    CP --> CP2[Examples: MongoDB, HBase, Spanner, etcd]

    AP --> AP1[Accept writes on both sides]
    AP --> AP2[Reconcile via vector clocks / LWW]
    AP --> AP3[Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak, Couchbase]

    style CP fill:#fcf,stroke:#606
    style AP fill:#cff,stroke:#066
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                  CAP TRIANGLE
                          C
                         / \
                        /   \
                       / CP  \  AP
                      /       \
                     /_________\
                    P     CA     A
                    (unavoidable
                     in real nets)

  Network partition splits 5 nodes into {A,B} and {C,D,E}:

     +---+ +---+      X partition      +---+ +---+ +---+
     | A | | B |      ============     | C | | D | | E |
     +-+-+ +-+-+      no traffic       +-+-+ +-+-+ +-+-+
       |   |          crosses            |   |   |
       +---+                             +---+---+
     minority side                     majority side

  CP choice : minority {A,B} refuse writes (cannot reach quorum)
              majority {C,D,E} keep serving → consistency preserved

  AP choice : both sides accept writes
              reconcile on heal (last-writer-wins or vector clocks)
```

### Walkthrough
1. A network partition divides the cluster into a minority side (2 nodes) and a majority side (3 nodes). Messages between the two sides are dropped or delayed.
2. A client writes to a node on the minority side. In a **CP** system, that node cannot reach a quorum, so it refuses the write — preserving consistency but sacrificing availability. In an **AP** system, the node accepts the write locally and returns success — preserving availability but risking divergent state.
3. When the partition heals, the **CP** system simply resumes normal operation. The **AP** system runs a reconciliation process (read-repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy) to converge the divergent writes — typically using last-writer-wins timestamps or application-provided merge functions.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
CAP theorem simulator.
Given a cluster config + a network partition, show what CP vs AP guarantees.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List, Dict

@dataclass
class Node:
    name: str
    data: Dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)   # key -> value
    reachable: set = field(default_factory=set)            # other reachable nodes

@dataclass
class Cluster:
    nodes: List[Node]
    quorum: int                # write must be acked by >= quorum nodes
    mode: str                  # 'CP' or 'AP'

def simulate_partition(cluster: Cluster, side_a: List[str], side_b: List[str]) -> Dict:
    """
    Partition nodes into side_a and side_b. Try to write on side_a.
    Returns per-node behavior.
    """
    names_a = set(side_a)
    names_b = set(side_b)

    # set reachability
    for n in cluster.nodes:
        n.reachable = set()
    for n in cluster.nodes:
        for m in cluster.nodes:
            if n.name == m.name:
                continue
            same_side = (n.name in names_a and m.name in names_a) or \
                        (n.name in names_b and m.name in names_b)
            if same_side:
                n.reachable.add(m.name)

    results = {}
    # try to write key="x", value="v_a" on a node in side_a
    writer = next(n for n in cluster.nodes if n.name in names_a)
    reachable_count = len(writer.reachable) + 1  # +self

    if cluster.mode == "CP":
        if reachable_count >= cluster.quorum:
            # majority side: can write
            writer.data["x"] = "v_a"
            for r in writer.reachable:
                cluster.nodes_dict[r].data["x"] = "v_a" if hasattr(cluster, 'nodes_dict') else None
            results["write_outcome"] = f"COMMITTED on {writer.name} (reachable={reachable_count} >= quorum={cluster.quorum})"
            results["guarantees"] = "Consistency preserved; Availability on minority side LOST"
        else:
            results["write_outcome"] = f"REJECTED on {writer.name} (reachable={reachable_count} < quorum={cluster.quorum})"
            results["guarantees"] = "Consistency preserved; Availability LOST on minority side"
    elif cluster.mode == "AP":
        # always accept the write locally
        writer.data["x"] = "v_a"
        for r in writer.reachable:
            rn = next(n for n in cluster.nodes if n.name == r)
            rn.data["x"] = "v_a"
        results["write_outcome"] = f"ACCEPTED locally on {writer.name} (will reconcile on heal)"
        results["guarantees"] = "Availability preserved; Consistency LOST until reconciliation"

    results["per_node_state"] = {n.name: dict(n.data) for n in cluster.nodes}
    return results

if __name__ == "__main__":
    nodes = [Node(f"N{i}") for i in range(5)]
    cluster_cp = Cluster(nodes=nodes, quorum=3, mode="CP")
    cluster_ap = Cluster(nodes=nodes, quorum=3, mode="AP")

    print("=== CP system: partition N0,N1 | N2,N3,N4 ===")
    r = simulate_partition(cluster_cp, side_a=["N0", "N1"], side_b=["N2", "N3", "N4"])
    for k, v in r.items():
        print(f"  {k}: {v}")

    print("\n=== AP system: same partition ===")
    # reset node data
    for n in nodes:
        n.data = {}
    r = simulate_partition(cluster_ap, side_a=["N0", "N1"], side_b=["N2", "N3", "N4"])
    for k, v in r.items():
        print(f"  {k}: {v}")

    print("\n=== Verdict ===")
    print("CP: writes blocked on minority side, data identical across all nodes once healed")
    print("AP: writes accepted everywhere, data DIVERGES until read-repair / anti-entropy runs")
```

quiz.explanation: Cassandra, descended from the Amazon Dynamo design, treats availability as paramount. Every replica accepts writes locally with no quorum requirement (default consistency level ONE), so during a partition every side keeps accepting writes — that is the "always writable" property. After the partition heals, Cassandra converges using three mechanisms.

options: CAP consistency means linearizability — every read sees the latest write, and the system behaves as if there is a single copy of the data even though it is replicated.

quiz.explanation: MongoDB replica sets elect a single primary that owns all writes; secondaries replicate the primary's oplog asynchronously. If the primary loses contact with a majority of secondaries (a partition leaves it on the minority side), it cannot prove it is still the leader, so it steps down and refuses writes.
